prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate economic shocks into credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) identified a specific, general mechanism: borrowing limits tied to asset values turn a small shock into a persistent, amplified fluctuation. The model became the template for the financial-friction literature and remains a building block of macro-financial models and of the policy discussion of leverage. The attribution is unusually clean, with one paper, two authors and no precursor who needs to be added. The colleagues who engaged with the attribution question mostly agree on this. My empirical case is more modest than in my opening statement. The mechanism has been taken up and tested in later work on collateral values, firm investment and credit supply, but I have not independently verified how strongly that work supports it, and I treat that support as suggestive rather than settled.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the original contribution is a stylised theoretical model. Its empirical standing rests largely on later work by other people, so the prize would reward the idea more than direct evidence of its quantitative importance. A second reservation is thematic. The 2022 prize covered banks and financial crises, and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator is a neighbouring line. Some members may therefore see this as a second award for the same theme. A third is practical. Opening support for this entry is narrower than for B001, so even if I judge the science to be clean, it may not be the entry that can command six votes.

responses.point: Andersson ranked B002 eighth. He argued that the 2022 prize partly covers the financial-crisis theme, that it is unclear whether Kiyotaki-Moore or the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator is the primary contribution, and that B002 competes with B001 for a macro slot.
responses.response: The 2022 overlap is a fair concern, but I read it differently. That prize recognised bank runs, bank intermediation and the Great Depression. Kiyotaki-Moore is a different mechanism, in which collateral values and asset prices drive amplification inside the real economy. On primacy, the accelerator and Kiyotaki-Moore are complementary strands. Only Kiyotaki-Moore is a single, identifiable origin paper with a clean authorship, which is why I limit the credit to two names and do not add Gertler and Gilchrist. I accept that the macro-slot competition is real, and for that reason I list B001 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Krusell ranked B001 first. He argued that Calvo, Taylor and Woodford are the most defensible three, that few macro contributions have comparable influence, and that the framework came through the post-2021 inflation episode damaged but standing. He ranked B002 fifth and described it as highly stylised, with mixed empirical quantification.
responses.response: His argument that the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio is separable changes my view. I had treated B001 as the most diffuse candidate, and eight of the eleven opening proposals converge on this trio, which lowers my attribution concern. I still differ with him on one point. Whether the framework came through the inflation episode intact depends on how one reads the Phillips curve evidence, and as someone who prioritises credible results over clear ones, I treat that as unresolved. I agree with him about the stylisation of Kiyotaki-Moore, and that is my main reservation about my own first choice. I have moved B001 up and now name it as an alternative.

responses.point: Teorell ranked B002 second. He called Kiyotaki-Moore the identifiable origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism and the cleanest attribution, but flagged that Gertler's overlap with the New Keynesian candidate makes his exclusion a judgement call and that the empirical content rests partly on calibrated models.
responses.response: I agree on the attribution, and the Gertler issue is a reason to prefer the two-name version. If Gertler were credited here he would also be a candidate in B001 and the credit would blur. Teorell's second point is a fair challenge to my opening wording that the mechanism has 'stood up well' empirically. Calibrated quantification is not the same as clean identification, and I now state that more cautiously. I would still say that the mechanism's relevance for collateral and credit supply has been examined in later work, though I have not verified how strong that evidence is.

responses.point: Hassler ranked B002 first alongside me. He stressed that it is a foundational, tractable and widely reused mechanism with ample time since its publication, but he acknowledged that direct empirical identification of collateral channels is more mixed than the theory's influence suggests.
responses.response: I agree with both parts of his assessment. The mixed identification is the point I would most want the Committee to weigh. A mechanism can be influential and conceptually deep while its quantitative importance is still disputed. Our shared first-place ranking should not count as evidence of merit. The test is whether the mechanism's central claim, that collateral-value feedback amplifies shocks, has survived scrutiny, and I would like colleagues who know the macro literature better than I do to say whether it has.

responses.point: Strömberg ranked B015 first. He argued that BLP and dynamic oligopoly estimation changed the measurement of demand and market power, and he raised whether Bresnahan or the entry-model contributions of Bresnahan and Reiss should displace Levinsohn.
responses.response: I ranked B015 second and still think the contribution is concrete and widely reused. His Bresnahan-versus-Levinsohn point is a real attribution problem, and Friberg raises the same question. Neither of us has resolved it. Because the three-name cap forces a choice that the opening evidence does not settle, I have moved B015 off my alternatives list. This is a judgement about attribution risk and not a lower view of the science.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises weighs against another financial-frictions award, or is seen as a distinct mechanism.
How strong the empirical support for the collateral-constraint channel is, given that it comes largely from later work by others and I have not independently verified it.
Whether B002 can attract enough support to reach six votes, or whether B001, where the trio of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford has drawn convergent proposals, is the more realistic macro candidate.
Whether the Committee would want a separate or additional credit for the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator line, and how that would interact with Gertler's place in B001.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the credited names in B002, B001 or B021. For transparency, my research on cooperation and costly punishment and on replication of laboratory experiments is topically adjacent to B004 (social preferences). I do not prefer B004 here and have no personal or institutional tie to its credited names. I have not verified any connection beyond what the profile states.
